name: Thematic Coding
title: Thematic Coding
answer: Thematic coding is the qualitative research practice of assigning short labels to segments of text, interview transcripts, field notes, open survey answers or documents, so that patterns of meaning can be identified and compared across a corpus. It sits inside qualitative analysis and mixed methods, where it feeds into framework analysis, grounded theory, content analysis and the later stages of interpretation. The unit of work is the code, a named idea attached to a passage, and the output is a codebook plus the coded material that supports it. Researchers use it whenever the question is about meaning, experience or framing rather than about measurement alone.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a document set, a coding frame and software that keeps codes attached to their source passages. Common environments include NVivo, ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA, Dedoose and Taguette, with spreadsheets and shared documents used for smaller studies. Transcripts arrive from recording and transcription tools, and mixed methods projects often join coded text to quantitative variables in the same dataset. Storage, access permissions and version history matter because coding is iterative and several coders may touch the same files over months.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical cycle starts with familiarisation, reading the material closely before any labels are applied. The researcher then generates initial codes, often line by line, and groups them into candidate themes, checking each theme against the extracts it claims to explain. Where several coders are involved, a subset of the material is coded independently and disagreements are discussed until the frame is stable, with agreement reported as a reliability figure. AI assistance now appears at several points, from suggesting candidate codes to clustering passages by similarity, but the interpretive judgement about what a passage means stays with the researcher.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main obligations are consent, confidentiality and an honest audit trail. Participants may be identifiable even after names are removed, so quotes need checking against context, and sensitive material needs restricted access. Provenance matters when software or a model proposes codes, because a reader should be able to see whether a theme came from the data, from the frame or from a tool. Reflexivity, positionality and clear documentation of how the frame changed over time are part of the method, not decoration. Where AI tools are used, their role and limits belong in the methods section.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward assisted rather than automated coding, with models used to draft candidate codes, retrieve similar passages and check consistency across large corpora. That shifts the researcher's time from mechanical labelling toward interpretation, comparison and writing, and it raises the bar for documenting how a theme was reached. Expect more work on transparent codebooks, on evaluating whether machine-suggested codes match human judgement, and on mixed methods designs that treat coded text as one input among several. The core skill, deciding what a passage means and defending that reading, is unlikely to move to a tool.
